Learning Whom to Trust with MACE

paper.acl.N13-1132

Prepared 15 Nov 2026 · Evidence snapshot 12 Nov 2026 · Report research-2026-11-12.1 · Evidence research-2026-11-11.candidate.1

Evidence & scope

Substantive bounded primary methods/results/limitations source review is documented at ACL-Anthology-N13-1132-captured-2026-11-10. Generative annotator/spammer assumptions and task-specific label aggregation make this a substantive methods work. Exact ACLN13-1132 identity is distinct from a version; older foundation membership remains protected and final scope-designation closure is separate. Original author/source-verifier/adversarial receipts bind every exact approved fact; unread pages, unreplicated experiments and source conflicts remain recorded in the pinned dossier. This admission is for one logical paper work only.

Approved findings

Approved evidence · As of 10 Nov 2026

The simple categorical model assumes an annotator is correct whenever not spamming and learns spamming biases independent of the true label; the authors acknowledge that this does not reflect the full reality of AMT, and do not model the continuous-label tasks.

Approved evidence · As of 10 Nov 2026

MACE models a binary spamming state per annotator-instance and an annotator-specific trust parameter, estimating unobserved true categorical labels with EM or variational Bayes; nonspamming annotations are assumed to copy the true label.

Approved evidence · As of 10 Nov 2026

Natural-data evaluation reused categorical AMT datasets from Snow et al.: word-sense disambiguation (177 items, 34 annotators), textual entailment (800, 164), and temporal relations (462, 76), with expert gold labels.

Approved evidence · As of 10 Nov 2026

At full coverage, Table 2 reports MACE-EM/VB accuracy 0.93 on RTE, 0.94 on temporal relations and 0.99 on WSD, compared with majority-vote 0.90, 0.93 and 0.99 respectively; lower-coverage thresholded results are explicitly not comparable at full coverage.
